subject: environmental-science
title: Captive Breeding and Reintroduction
welcome_lead: Arabian oryx, California condor, golden lion tamarin — stories of return.
meta_desc: A-Level Environmental Science adventure on captive breeding and reintroduction programmes.
final_note: Ex situ alone is insufficient — habitat must await the return of revived populations.

concepts.def: Conservation outside natural habitat (zoos, botanical gardens, seed banks).
Conservation within natural habitat (reserves, protected areas).
Extinct in wild 1972; reintroduced from captive stock; now Vulnerable (IUCN).
Pedigree record minimising inbreeding in captive populations.
Average relatedness used to prioritise breeding pairs.
Storage of crop and wild plant seeds (e.g., Svalbard Global Seed Vault).

walkthroughs.body_html: Studbooks track every individual. Breeding pairs minimise kinship to retain diversity over generations.
Arabian oryx reintroduced to Oman, Saudi Arabia, Israel. California condor recovered from 22 individuals (1987) to >500.
Captive populations risk genetic adaptation to artificial environments, reducing wild fitness. Pre-release training mitigates.

mcqs.q: The Arabian oryx programme is significant because:
options: It restored a species extinct in the wild via captive breeding
Select breeding pairs that minimise inbreeding

numericals.q: If a captive population has 30 founders contributing equally, the mean inbreeding coefficient after one generation of random mating is ≈ 1/(2N). Calculate (3 d.p.).

free_texts.q: Name the seed-bank facility on the Norwegian archipelago that safeguards global crop genetic diversity (two words).
